chapters.name: Chapter 1: Principles and bringing land back

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Agroecology: principles you can use on your farm
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Match practices on your farm to the principles of agroecology.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of practices on your farm, you will match each practice to the agroecology principle it uses, such as recycling, diversity or synergies, matching at least five practices correctly.
Agroecology means farming with the way nature works: using plants, animals, soil life, trees and people's knowledge so the farm feeds itself more and buys in less. FAO describes 10 elements of agroecology, adopted by its member countries in 2019.
Five are about how the farm works: recycling (nutrients and waste go back into the farm), efficiency (more from the same water, land and inputs), diversity (many crops, animals and trees), synergies (parts that help each other, like legumes feeding maize) and resilience (coping with shocks). Five are about people: co-creation of knowledge (farmers and researchers learning together), human and social values, culture and food traditions, responsible governance, and circular and solidarity economy (selling and buying locally and fairly).
You probably use some already. Feeding maize stover to goats and putting their manure back on the field is recycling and synergy. Intercropping cassava with groundnuts is diversity. A farmer field school is co-creation of knowledge. Agroecology asks you to use these on purpose, and to add more, step by step.
Words to know:
- Agroecology: farming that uses natural processes and local knowledge so the farm needs fewer bought inputs and copes better with shocks.
- Synergy: when two parts of the farm help each other, so together they give more than apart.
- Recycling (on a farm): returning crop residues, manure and waste to the soil instead of losing them.
Official sources:
- FAO: The 10 elements of agroecology (adopted by FAO members in 2019)
- FAO: Agroecology Knowledge Hub
Try it now: List six practices on your farm or in your village. Next to each, write the agroecology principle it uses (recycling, efficiency, diversity, synergies, resilience or one of the people elements). Circle one principle you hardly use.
You can now match farm practices to the principles of agroecology and spot which ones you could use more.

check.q: A farmer feeds bean haulms to her goats and spreads the goat manure on her maize. Which principles is she using?
check.why: Residues feed the animals and manure feeds the soil: nutrients are recycled and the parts help each other.

check.q: Which is an example of diversity on a farm?
options: Only maize, every season, on every field
Cassava, groundnuts, trees and goats on the same farm
check.why: Many crops, animals and trees together is diversity, one of FAO's 10 elements.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Bringing degraded land back: cover crops and green manure
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose a cover crop or green manure for a degraded field and plan when to sow and cut it.
This lesson builds toward: For one degraded field, you will choose a cover crop or green manure and plan when to sow it and when to cut it back, with a species that fits your rainfall and a sowing and cutting date.
Degraded land has lost organic matter and structure: rain runs off, crops are stunted and weeds such as striga take over. Mulch and compost help, but you rarely have enough. Cover crops and green manures grow the organic matter on the field itself.
A cover crop is grown mainly to cover and protect the soil, often between seasons. A green manure is grown and then cut and left on or worked into the soil to feed it. Legumes do both and also add nitrogen: lablab, mucuna (velvet bean), canavalia (jack bean), crotalaria, cowpea and pigeon pea are used in different parts of Africa. Some, like lablab and cowpea, also give food or fodder; mucuna seed needs special processing before people can eat it, so treat it as a soil and feed crop and ask extension.
Leafy shrubs can be used as green leaf manure too. In western Kenya, farmers cut tithonia (Mexican sunflower) leaves from hedges and spread them on fields; research found the leaves rich in nutrients, but cutting and carrying is hard work, so it pays best on vegetables and other high-value crops.
Timing matters. Sow the cover crop early enough to grow well before the dry season, or relay it into the main crop a few weeks after planting. Cut it back before it competes with your next crop or sets hard seed, and leave the cut material on the surface as mulch. Ask your extension officer or research institute which species and dates suit your rainfall.
Step by step:
- Walk the field: where is it bare, hard or full of striga?
- Choose one or two cover crop or green manure species that fit your rainfall.
- Decide: grow it between seasons, relay it into the main crop, or as a fallow.
- Write the sowing date and the cutting date.
- Cut before it competes with your crop; leave it on the surface.
- Keep animals off until it has done its job, or plan a fodder share.
Words to know:
- Degraded land: land that has lost soil, organic matter or plant cover, so it produces much less.
- Cover crop: a crop grown mainly to cover and protect the soil.
- Green manure: a crop grown and then cut and left on or in the soil to feed it.
- Relay cropping: sowing a second crop into a standing crop before the first is harvested.
Official sources:
- Tithonia diversifolia: variations in leaf nutrient concentration and implications for biomass transfer (western Kenya)
- FAO: The importance of soil organic matter
Try it now: Pick your most degraded field. Choose one cover crop or green manure for it, and write: why you chose it, the sowing date, how you will sow it (between seasons, relay or fallow) and the cutting date. Note one question to ask your extension officer.
You can now choose a cover crop or green manure for a degraded field and plan when to sow and cut it.

check.q: What is the main difference between a cover crop and a green manure?
options: Green manures are bought in bags
A green manure is grown to be cut and left to feed the soil
check.why: Cover crops protect the soil; green manures are grown mainly to be cut and feed it (many crops do both).

check.q: When should you cut back a cover crop grown before maize?
options: Before it competes with the maize or sets hard seed
check.why: Cutting at the right time stops competition and leaves mulch for the next crop.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Trees that come back: FMNR and fertilizer trees
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan farmer-managed natural regeneration or fertilizer trees for one plot.
This lesson builds toward: On a plot with living tree stumps or space for trees, you will plan farmer-managed natural regeneration or fertilizer trees, step by step, covering which stumps or trees, how many stems, pruning and protection from animals and fire.
Many fields that look treeless still have living tree stumps and roots under the soil. Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR) lets them grow back instead of slashing them every season. In Niger, FMNR spread from farmer to farmer and has brought trees back to more than five million hectares of farmland, giving fodder, firewood, shade and better crops.
The steps, from World Vision and partner guides: survey the field for sprouting stumps and choose the useful species; for each stump, keep three to five of the tallest, straightest stems and cut the rest; prune side branches up to about halfway up each stem, with a sharp tool, cutting upwards; come back every few months to remove new shoots; protect the stems from animals and fire; when you harvest a stem, let a younger one replace it. Mark the chosen stems and agree rules with your neighbours and community so animals and cutters leave them alone.
Where there are no stumps, you can plant fertilizer trees: legume trees such as gliricidia, faidherbia (common in Sahel parklands, including Senegal's groundnut basin) or calliandra, whose leaves feed the soil or animals. Long trials in Malawi and Zambia found maize grown with gliricidia gave steadier yields over the years than maize with fertilizer alone, though pruning the trees two or three times a year is real work.
Before cutting or selling trees, check your country's forestry rules and your community's by-laws.
Step by step:
- Walk the plot and mark living stumps and young trees.
- Choose useful species: fodder, fuel, fruit, soil.
- Keep 3 to 5 straight stems per stump; cut the rest.
- Prune side branches halfway up; sharp tool, cut upwards.
- Protect from animals and fire; agree rules with neighbours.
- No stumps? Plan fertilizer trees with extension advice.
Words to know:
- FMNR: farmer-managed natural regeneration: letting tree stumps and roots on your land grow back, then choosing and pruning the best stems.
- Fertilizer tree: a tree, usually a legume, whose leaves feed the soil.
- Parkland: farmland with trees scattered across the fields.
- By-law: a rule agreed by a local community or council.
Official sources:
- Tearfund Footsteps 110: Farmer-managed natural regeneration, steps to success (with World Vision)
- World Agroforestry (ICRAF) Uganda: FMNR user guide
- Sileshi et al.: Can integration of legume trees increase yield stability in rain-fed maize cropping systems in Southern Africa? (Malawi and Zambia trials)
- FAO: Agroforestry
Try it now: Walk one plot and count the living stumps or young trees. Draw a quick sketch marking the ones you would keep. Write which species they are (or ask someone), what you want from them, and how you will protect them from animals and fire.
You can now plan farmer-managed natural regeneration or fertilizer trees for a plot, step by step.

check.q: In FMNR, what do you do with the many shoots on a living stump?
options: Keep three to five of the tallest, straightest stems and cut the rest
check.why: Keeping a few good stems lets them grow fast into useful trees.

check.q: Why should a farmer agree FMNR rules with neighbours?
options: So animals and woodcutters leave the chosen stems alone
Because trees grow faster after a meeting
check.why: Community agreement protects the stems from grazing and cutting while they grow.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: A farm that feeds itself

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Crops, livestock and biodiversity working together
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw the flows of feed, manure and residues between your crops and animals.
This lesson builds toward: Given the crops and animals on your farm, you will draw the flows of feed, manure and residues between your crops and animals, showing at least three links and one place where nutrients leave the farm.
On a mixed farm, crops and animals can feed each other. Crop residues, cover crops, tree leaves and grain by-products feed animals; animals turn them into milk, meat, eggs, draught power and manure; manure and urine go back to feed the soil. When those links are strong, less money leaves the farm.
Draw it. Put your fields, animals, home and compost or manure heap on paper, then draw arrows: stover to goats, manure to the vegetable plot, chicken litter to the compost, pond water to the vegetables in a fish farm. Then mark the leaks: residues burned, manure left in the sun and rain, urine lost, produce sold without anything coming back. Each leak is a place to gain.
Biodiversity is part of the system too. Trees, hedges, grass strips and flowering plants give homes to the insects and birds that eat pests and to the bees that pollinate beans, tomatoes and coffee. Different crops and varieties spread risk. Keep some wild corners, avoid spraying when you do not need to, and grow more than one crop.
Watch the balance: animals need feed through the dry season, and residues used for feed are not on the soil as mulch. Decide what share goes where, and grow extra fodder (grass strips, fodder trees, lablab) so you do not have to choose.
Step by step:
- Draw your fields, animals, home and manure heap.
- Draw arrows for each flow: feed, residues, manure, water.
- Mark the leaks: burning, lost manure and urine, nothing returned.
- Mark places for biodiversity: hedges, trees, flowers, wild corners.
- Pick one leak to close this season.
Words to know:
- Mixed farming: growing crops and keeping animals on the same farm so they support each other.
- Nutrient flow: how nutrients move around the farm, for example from feed to manure to soil.
- Biodiversity: the variety of plants, animals, insects and soil life on and around the farm.
- Natural enemies: insects, birds and other animals that eat crop pests.
Official sources:
- FAO: The 10 elements of agroecology (adopted by FAO members in 2019)
- FAO: Agroforestry
Try it now: Draw your farm's flow map with at least three arrows between crops and animals. Mark at least one leak and one place where you could add biodiversity. Write the one leak you will close this season.
You can now draw the flows of feed, manure and residues on your farm and find the leaks to close.

check.q: On a flow map, which of these is a leak?
options: Manure spread on the vegetable plot
Manure left in the sun and rain until it washes away
check.why: Manure exposed to sun and rain loses nutrients that should go back to the soil.

check.q: Why keep hedges, trees and flowering plants around fields?
options: They house natural enemies of pests and pollinators
check.why: Habitat for pest eaters and bees is a free service to your crops.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Cutting the cost of imported fertilizer
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Estimate how many bags of bought fertilizer on-farm nutrients can replace, and the money saved.
This lesson builds toward: Given last season's fertilizer use, you will estimate how many bags of bought fertilizer on-farm nutrients can replace and the money saved, in local currency, marked as an estimate to check with extension.
Most mineral fertilizer used in Africa is imported, so its price follows world markets and exchange rates. Agroecology aims to need less of it, not always none. Start from what you used last season: how many bags, which type, on which field, and what they cost.
Then list the on-farm nutrients you can add: legume cover crops and intercrops (nitrogen), fertilizer trees and green leaf manure, more and better-kept manure and urine, bio-slurry if you have a biodigester, and crop residues kept on the field. Combining a smaller amount of mineral fertilizer with these often works better than either alone. In the Malawi trials, maize with gliricidia plus half the recommended fertilizer did about as well as maize with the full rate.
Estimate, then test. For example (made-up figures): a farmer in Kakamega used 4 bags on one acre at KES 3,500 a bag. With a lablab relay crop and more manure, she plans to try 2 bags on half the field and 4 on the other half, and compare yields. If the yields match, she saves 2 bags, KES 7,000, on that acre. Do not cut fertilizer suddenly on all your land.
Ask your extension officer or soil lab to check your plan against your soil results, and buy mineral fertilizer only from registered agro-dealers in sealed bags.
Step by step:
- Write last season's fertilizer: bags, type, field, cost.
- List the on-farm nutrients you can add.
- Plan a reduced rate on part of a field, with on-farm nutrients.
- Keep a full-rate strip to compare.
- Estimate the bags and money saved if yields hold.
- Check the plan with extension; scale up only what works.
Words to know:
- Mineral fertilizer: manufactured fertilizer, such as urea, DAP or NPK, usually sold in bags.
- Integrated soil fertility management: combining organic nutrients (manure, legumes, residues) with a smaller amount of mineral fertilizer.
- Comparison strip: a part of the field farmed the old way so you can compare results fairly.
Official sources:
- Sileshi et al.: Can integration of legume trees increase yield stability in rain-fed maize cropping systems in Southern Africa? (Malawi and Zambia trials)
- 4R Plant Nutrient Management in African Agriculture: an extension handbook
Try it now: Write last season's fertilizer use for one field. List two on-farm nutrient sources you will add. Plan a half-field test with a lower rate, and estimate the bags and money you would save if yields hold, in your currency.
You can now estimate how much bought fertilizer on-farm nutrients could replace, and plan a fair test before you cut.

check.q: You want to use less fertilizer. What is the safest first step?
options: Stop all fertilizer on every field at once
Buy unlabelled fertilizer because it is cheaper
Test a lower rate plus on-farm nutrients on part of a field, beside a full-rate strip
check.why: A side-by-side test shows whether the lower rate works before you risk the whole harvest.

check.q: A farmer in Nigeria used 6 bags at NGN 40,000 each and cuts to 4 with the same yield. What did he save?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring improvement over seasons
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Record simple soil and farm measures at the same time each season.
This lesson builds toward: On the field you are restoring, you will record simple soil and farm measures at the same time each season, using at least four measures, written down and compared with the season before. For one degraded field, you will choose a cover crop or green manure and plan when to sow it and when to cut it back, with a species that fits your rainfall and a sowing and cutting date. Given last season's fertilizer use, you will estimate how many bags of bought fertilizer on-farm nutrients can replace and the money saved, in local currency, marked as an estimate to check with extension.
Regeneration is slow. Yields may not jump in the first season, so you need other signs to see whether the soil is coming back. Measure the same spots, in the same month, every season, and write it down.
Simple measures: ground cover (how much of the soil is covered by plants or mulch; estimate by eye or count in a square); earthworms (dig a spade-sized block and count); infiltration (push a tin with both ends cut into the soil, pour in water and time how long it takes to soak in); soil smell and crumb (does it break into small crumbs or big hard clods?); a soil photo from the same spot; the yield from a marked plot; and the fertilizer bags and money you spent.
Every few years, a lab soil test can show organic matter and nutrients (see "Soil Health and Fertility" for sampling). Compare your restored field with an unchanged one if you can.
A phone helps: take photos from the same spot, keep your numbers in a notes app or spreadsheet, and ask an AI assistant to turn them into a simple table or chart. The numbers come from your field.
Step by step:
- Mark three spots in the field with sticks or stones.
- Choose at least four measures: cover, worms, infiltration, crumb, photo, yield, cost.
- Record them in the same month each season.
- Compare with last season and with an unchanged field.
- Review your plan: keep what works, change what does not.
Words to know:
- Indicator: a simple sign you measure to see whether things are getting better or worse.
- Infiltration: how quickly water soaks into the soil.
- Ground cover: the share of the soil surface covered by plants or mulch.
- Baseline: your first measurement, which later ones are compared with.
Official sources:
- FAO: The importance of soil organic matter
- FAO: Agroecology Knowledge Hub
Try it now: Final task: write your three-season regeneration plan for one field, with a sketch. Then take your baseline today: mark three spots and record at least four measures (for example cover, worm count, infiltration time and a photo).
You can now measure your soil and farm with simple indicators each season and use them to judge your regeneration plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Principles named The plan does not say which agroecology principles it uses. Each practice in the plan is linked to an agroecology principle. Uses at least four different principles, including one of the people elements. Cover crop or green manure No cover crop or green manure, or no dates. A species that fits the rainfall, with sowing and cutting dates. Also explains how it fits with animal feed and the main crop, and was checked with extension. Trees No tree plan, or trees with no protection. FMNR or fertilizer trees with stems or species, pruning and protection from animals and fire. Includes a community agreement or by-law, and how stems will be harvested and replaced. Crop-livestock links No flow map, or only one link. A flow map with at least three links and one leak to close. Shows how residues are shared between feed and mulch and where biodiversity is added. Fertilizer saving No estimate, or plans to stop fertilizer on all land at once. Estimates bags and money saved in local currency, with a fair test against a full-rate strip. Plan checked with extension or soil results, with a rule for when to scale up. Measures over seasons No measures or no baseline. At least four measures, a baseline taken and a date for each season. Includes an unchanged comparison field and photos from fixed spots. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and try again.

check.q: Why measure the same spots in the same month every season?
options: So the comparison is fair and shows real change
Because worms only appear in one month
check.why: Same place and time remove other causes, so changes reflect the soil.

check.q: Water in your infiltration tin soaks in faster than last year. What does it suggest?
options: Soil structure is improving and holding more rain
check.why: Faster infiltration means more rain goes into the soil instead of running off.
